schools.summary: Gill: though Job neither names nor addresses his friends, he desires only to have his cause laid before God, by whom he would be acquitted; the chapter proves a righteous man may be afflicted by God's unchangeable decree, a sufficient answer to Eliphaz.
Ellicott: Job answers the insinuations of Eliphaz with earnest longing after God and the assertion of his innocence, and in ch. 24 laments that his case is but one of many.
Henry: sure he has been wronged, Job will not give up the cause nor let the friends have the last word, but appeals from their censures to the just judgment of God.
Clarke maps the whole speech: Job apologizes for complaining, longs to plead before his Maker but cannot find him, gives himself up to God with conviction of innocence, yet fears God's majesty.

themes: the frame of the whole speech

schools.summary: Gill keeps the AV 'bitter': not a charge of injustice but a lament over afflictions too heavy for his strength and a God who hides his face — bitter as the waters of Marah.

Wesley: the stroke, God's hand upon him, exceeds his groaning; Clarke presses Mr. Good's 'And still is my complaint rebellion?' — the friends construe his laments as rebellion, and מרי may derive from מרה, 'he rebelled.'

Keil and Delitzsch note מרי usually means obstinacy/rebellion ('my complaint still biddeth defiance'), weighing the LXX's 'from his hand'; Ellicott gives both — 'bitter, or accounted rebellion' — with 'my stroke heavier than my groaning' the agreed clause.

sides.position: 'bitter' — a lament, no just measure of his suffering, not a charge against God
'rebellion/defiance' — the complaint the friends account mutiny
the word bears both, 'bitter, or accounted rebellion'

themes: the stroke heavier than the groaning

schools.summary: Gill supplies the unnamed 'him' (God) and, with Jarchi, reads 'his seat' as the Judge's throne; Job, under the hidings of God's face, knows not 'how' (Broughton) to find the God who is everywhere.
Henry hears a deserted soul longing to recover God's favour and covenant — 'Saw you him whom my soul loveth?' — yet complaining too boldly, as if to demand justice at the seat.
Clarke reads a forensic wish: 'Who will give me the knowledge of God, that I may find him out? ... exhibit my judgment before his face, and fill my mouth with convincing arguments.'
Ellicott: the piteous complaint of a man who feels God is with him for chastisement, but not for healing.

themes: Oh that I knew where I might find him
the longing of a clear conscience

schools.summary: Gill allows a double setting — the language of prayer directed and set in order, or of a defendant justifying not his person by works but his cause, clearing the aspersions as Samuel once vindicated himself.
Keil and Delitzsch keep the forensic image — 'I would lay the cause before Him, and fill my mouth with arguments' — the speech of a man who longs not to escape the trial but to open it.

Henry turns it to prayer: liberty of access and of speech — to be particular (order our cause) and importunate (fill our mouths with arguments), not to move God but to move ourselves and excite faith.

themes: I would order my cause before him
the cause, not the person, justified

schools.summary: Gill: Job would then know the reason God contended with him and what his sins were — the very thing he has all along desired to be told.

Wesley: if God discovered secret sins, Job would humble himself and accept the punishment; Clarke: God would speak nothing but truth, decree nothing unrighteous, utter nothing Job could not comprehend.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'I should like to know the words He would answer me, and attend to what He would say' — a man who wants the decisive word from God, not the last word for himself.
Henry: Job knew the friends would only condemn him, but 'I would fain know what God would answer me, for his judgment is according to truth, which theirs is not.'

themes: the words he would answer me

schools.summary: Gill: God does not plead against his people but for them, not with great strength to crush nor by strict rigour of justice; whatever he does with the vessels of wrath, he deals otherwise with the vessels of mercy.

Clarke: God would not strike Job dumb by majesty but put strength in him, tempering rigid justice by equity, so mercy conducts all to the best issue; Wesley: he would use his power for Job, not against him, judging with the clemency he shows his children.

Ellicott: 'Would he contend with me in the greatness of his power? Nay; but he would have regard unto me' — Eliphaz bid Job acquaint himself with God (22:23); Job longs for nothing more than God's presence.

Henry: keep good thoughts of God — against the obstinate he pleads with great power, but with his own he deals in tender compassion, the same strength engaged for humble saints who prevail by strength derived from him, as Jacob did.

themes: will he plead with his great power?
he would put strength in me
God for his people, not against them

schools.summary: Gill takes 'there' of God's seat (mercy- or judgment-seat) and 'the righteous' of Job himself, who, conscious of his sincerity, fears not to reason his case before God.

Keil and Delitzsch weigh שׁם (local 'there' or temporal 'then') and decide temporal — then an upright man would be proved able to plead with God — reading 'I should for ever be delivered'; Ellicott hears a Gospel height: God the Saviour the refuge from God the Judge, all things working for good (Rom. 8:28).

Clarke owns 'to dispute with God sounds very harsh,' and reports Good's 'triumphantly should I escape,' since the word for 'for ever' may be 'to victory' (Vulgate); Wesley alone judges the wish irreverent, a speech for which God later reproves Job.

debates.question: Is Job's wish to dispute with God the boldness of a clear conscience or an irreverence God will rebuke?

sides.position: the holy confidence of an innocent man; God the Saviour is the refuge from God the Judge
an irreverence toward God for which he is afterwards reproved, and abhors himself

outliers.note: Judges 'so should I be delivered for ever from my judge' and the like expressions to savour of irreverence toward God, for which the Lord afterwards reproves Job, and Job abhors himself.

themes: delivered for ever / escape to victory
God the Saviour the refuge from God the Judge

schools.summary: Gill hears Job returning to v.3, relating his fruitless search; reports (but only as one man's fancy) Cocceius's turn that 'forward/backward' are times future and past.

Clarke: the verses paint a soul searching for God's favour — no means untried, no place unexplored, a true picture of a genuine penitent; Wesley: God is 'not there' only as a Judge, being essentially present in all places.
Keil and Delitzsch keep to the Hebrew — what is 'with' a man inwardly is what he thinks, knows, and wills — preparing the turn at v.10 where God's inward knowledge answers Job's failure to find him.
Henry gathers three losses: Job cannot fix his thoughts, cannot find the cause of his troubles, and cannot foresee the end — bewildered, not unbelieving.

outliers.note: Takes 'forward' and 'backward' as times future and past — Job looking to the days of the Messiah, his living Redeemer, and back to the first promise to Adam — which Gill relays only as a fancy.

themes: I go forward, but he is not there

schools.summary: Clarke maps the four cardinal points by a man facing sunrise — qedem 'before' (E), achor 'after' (W), semol 'left' (N), yamin 'right' (S) — and notes the south is scarcely visible in Idumea, the 'hidden chambers of the south' (ch. 9:9).

Gill takes 'the left hand where he doth work' of the north, where God stretched out the empty place; God works everywhere but more eminently in some regions — yet what Job meant by his 'work' in the north Gill owns is not easy to say.

themes: on the left hand where he doth work
the four cardinal points of Hebrew
the whole horizon searched in vain

schools.summary: Gill: though Job cannot find God, God knows his way — either the way of acceptance, his living Redeemer, or (more likely) the course of his conversation — and knows it not barely by omniscience but by approbation.

Clarke reads the refiner's image: like true gold Job loses nothing in the fire; genuine gold neither alters nor diminishes but comes out gold, as Job will come out of affliction the innocent man he went in.

Henry finds the resting-place of the labyrinth: 'Though I know not the way he takes, he knows the way I take' — acquainted with it and approving it — and infers three comforts: tried, come forth, and come forth as gold.

themes: he knoweth the way that I take
tried, I shall come forth as gold

schools.summary: Gill reads a close, constant imitation: Job trod in the very steps God walked in — holiness, righteousness, mercy — and persisted in them, walking worthy of him.

Wesley: 'his steps' are the paths God appointed men to walk in; Clarke: Job was not only generally but particularly religious, and lingers over Coverdale's 'hye strete,' the paved highway (via strata) of God's commandments kept and not forsaken.
Henry hears in 'held' and 'kept' a hard-won perseverance: the tempter used every art to draw him aside, yet by grace he held with resolution and kept with watchfulness.

themes: my foot hath held his steps
the high street of the commandments

schools.summary: Gill takes 'the commandment of his lips' broadly — Job living before Sinai — of any command God gave to Noah, Abraham, or the patriarchs, which Job kept as the rule of his walk.

Henry: Job would not go back from that commandment, and esteemed God's words more than his necessary food — 'laid it up' as provision against a siege; the word is to the soul what food is to the body (cf. 22:22).
Clarke prefers Good's 'in my bosom have I stored up the words of his mouth,' the Asiatics carrying what is precious in the bosom.
Ellicott notes the LXX and Vulgate read 'in my bosom,' but offers 'according to the statute prescribed to me' / 'from my own law,' and sets 'more than my necessary food' beside John 4:32-34.

debates.question: What does the last clause say of chukki?

sides.position: 'more than my necessary food' — the appointed portion (AV)
'in my bosom have I stored them' (Good, LXX, Vulgate)
'according to the statute prescribed to me / my own law' — a fixed principle to hoard God's words

themes: the word dearer than daily bread

schools.summary: Gill offers two references for 'in one mind' — God's commandments unaltered, or (more likely) his dealings with Job continued despite his innocence, since God is sovereign, unchangeable, and not to be wrought upon.

Henry: God's counsels are immutable — 'he is one with himself,' with no counsellors, never altering his measures; prayer changes his providence but never his purpose — and his power is irresistible, 'what his soul desires, that he does.'
Clarke reads the Hebrew 'but he is in one' as the Vulgate's 'he alone is' / Coverdale's 'it is he himself alone': God has no partner, his designs his own, none turning his determinations aside.
Ellicott holds both open: Job declares either God's unique sovereignty (he is one, alone) or his unchangeableness (of one mind).

debates.question: Does 'he is in one' mean God is unchangeable ('one mind') or unique ('alone, one')?

sides.position: 'in one mind' — an unchangeable purpose none can turn
'he is one/alone' — without partner or rival (Vulgate, Coverdale)
either — his unique sovereignty or his unchangeableness

themes: the will no creature can withstand

schools.summary: Gill notes the word for 'the thing appointed' is that of v.12 ('my necessary food'), some rendering 'he performeth my necessary things' (Targum, Broughton) — the earlier ambiguity following into this verse.

Clarke reads it as a portion or lot: 'he hath appointed me my lot, and like these there are multitudes with him' — God diversifies affairs, scarcely two men with the same lot; Wesley: God performs the calamities he has allotted, and there are 'many such' examples.

Ellicott renders 'he will accomplish my appointed lot ... and like these things there are many more with him' (cf. 10:13), catching Job's courage to take the full measure of the worst and still trust God (cf. 13:15).

Henry: it is God that performs it, all that and only that appointed, in the appointed time and method; the God who appointed us to glory appointed this affliction in the way, and 'many such things' mean our case is not singular (1 Pet. 5:9).

themes: he performeth the thing appointed for me
many such things are with him
bowing to a decreed lot in trust

schools.summary: Gill: not the gracious presence Job sought but God's appearance as enemy and as Judge; desiring the trial, he yet shrinks back at God's sovereignty, immutable counsels, and knowledge, not knowing what may be brought against him.
Clarke: Job sees no end to his sufferings — God has not exhausted his means of trial — and it is considering this that makes him afraid.

Ellicott draws the paradox: afraid of God yet longing to see him, conscious of his presence yet unable to find him — Job's history was to the old world what the Gospel is to the new, a righteous man made perfect through suffering.

Henry marks the bad use of good truths — 'Therefore am I troubled' where he might have said 'Therefore am I easy' — and the self-contradiction of being troubled at God's absence and now at his presence.

themes: trouble at God's absence and at his presence

schools.summary: Gill: not the penitent's contrite heart but a weak, fearful heart, pressed and broken under affliction, become as water and melting like wax, ready to faint and die away.
Clarke: God has prostrated Job's strength and deprived him of courage, so he sinks beneath his burden and is troubled at the very thought of the Almighty.

Ellicott unfolds two things — that God did not cut him off before the darkness, or hid it not from his eyes (cf. 3:11, 3:20), of physical suffering or mental distress; Keil and Delitzsch give the plain rendering, God has made his heart faint.
Henry distinguishes a gracious softness (Josiah, trembling at God's word) from this grievous softness, in which the troubled heart can bear nothing, afraid of everything present and future.

themes: a grievous, not a gracious, softness
the melting of fear, not repentance

schools.summary: Gill: Job is amazed, half wishing, that he was not cut off by death before the darkness came — as the righteous are taken from the evil to come — reporting Aben Ezra's reading as a wish, 'why was I not cut off?'

Wesley: God did not cut him off before these miseries came, nor cover him by the grave; Clarke reads altogether otherwise (Good's 'why can I not draw darkness over my face?') — it is not the evils but the fear of God's majesty that overwhelms Job, unbearable without a Mediator.

Henry hears the peevish side — Job quarrelling both that he did not die before his troubles and that he was left so long in them — yet adds that to the upright a marvellous light sometimes arises in the darkness.
Ellicott, holding the words to v.16, takes them of the two respects in which God troubled him — not cut off before the darkness, or the darkness not hidden from his face.

debates.question: How is the closing verse to be read?

sides.position: 'not cut off before the darkness' — Job wishes death had spared him the sight of his sorrows, or hidden him in the grave
'why can I not draw darkness over my face?' — it is not his sufferings but the terror of God's majesty that overwhelms him
the two respects — not cut off before the darkness, or the darkness not hidden from his face

themes: not cut off before the darkness
